fields.use: This test measures key monoamine metabolites in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), including 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), homovanillic acid (HVA) and 3-O-methyl-DOPA (3-OMD). It is used to support the diagnosis of disorders affecting dopamine and serotonin metabolism in the brain, particularly in pediatric patients.; Abnormal levels of these metabolites can indicate disruptions in neurotransmitter pathways. fields.use: Plasma 3-0-methyldopa (3-OMD) is useful for the diagnosis of Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) deficiency, a pyridoxal 5’-phosphate dependent enzyme responsible for the formation of dopamine and serotonin. This test may also support interpretation of variants of uncertain significance (VUS) identified through genetic testing, including next-generation sequencing, in the DDC gene and genes involved in pyridoxal 5’-phosphate metabolism. AADC deficiency is a congenital autosomal recessive metabolic disorder that causes hypotonia, hypokinesia, oculogyric crises and signs of autonomic dysfunction beginning in infancy. In AADC deficiency, L-dopa accumulates and can be methylated by catechol O-methyltransferase using S-adenosylmethionine as the methyl donor to form 3-OMD. 3-OMD is more stable than L-dopa and is elevated in plasma from patients with AADC deficiency.; Plasma 3-OMD may also be useful for assessing compliance and therapeutic monitoring of treatment with levodopa.

fields.use: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) lactate is an adjunctive test that may help differentiate bacterial meningitis from aseptic (typically viral) meningitis. CSF lactate is produced primarily within the central nervous system through anaerobic glycolysis and is largely independent of blood lactate concentrations. Elevated CSF lactate levels, particularly >3.9 mmol/L, are suggestive of bacterial meningitis, while lower concentrations are more consistent with aseptic meningitis. Results should always be interpreted in conjunction with CSF cell count and differential, protein, glucose, microbiologic culture, molecular testing and clinical findings.; Because elevated CSF lactate is not specific for bacterial meningitis, increased concentrations may also be observed in other neurologic conditions associated with cerebral hypoxia or impaired oxidative metabolism, including stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, traumatic brain injury, cerebral edema, seizure disorders and certain inborn errors of metabolism.
fields.limitations: CSF lactate concentrations may decrease following initiation of antimicrobial therapy. When bacterial meningitis is suspected, CSF specimens should ideally be collected before antibiotic administration to maximize diagnostic utility.

fields.use: CSF pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP), the active form of vitamin B6, is useful for evaluating disorders associated with reduced central nervous system PLP availability. PLP is an essential cofactor for numerous enzymes involved in neurotransmitter and amino acid metabolism. ; CSF PLP measurement may aid in the diagnosis of inherited disorders affecting vitamin B6 metabolism, including pyridox(am)ine 5'-phosphate oxidase (PNPO) deficiency, ALDH7A1 (antiquitin) deficiency and hyperprolinemia type II and Hyperphosphatasia with Mental Retardation Syndrome (HPMRS, Mabry Syndrome).
fields.specialInstructions: This test currently is not approved for use in New York state.
fields.limitations: Normal CSF PLP concentrations do not exclude all vitamin B6-related disorders. Some conditions impair intracellular PLP utilization without consistently lowering measurable CSF PLP levels. In addition, treatment status and disease heterogeneity may result in normal CSF PLP concentrations despite an underlying defect in vitamin B6 metabolism. Therefore, results should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings, complementary biochemical markers and molecular genetic testing.

fields.use: CSF Succinyladenosine is useful for diagnosing adenylosuccinate lyase (ADSL) deficiency, an autosomal recessive defect of purine metabolism. Clinical indications for testing include late or early onset seizures, delayed development of mental and movement abilities, autistic behavior, and encephalopathy with an occasional lack of myelination.; There are three forms of adenylosuccinate lyase deficiency:; 1. The neonatal form, the most severe form, can show signs and symptoms before birth, including impaired growth during fetal development and microcephaly. Newborns have severe encephalopathy, lack of movement, difficulty feeding, life-threatening respiratory problems and intractable seizures.; 2. Adenylosuccinate lyase deficiency type I is the most common form. Signs and symptoms present in the first months of life and include severe psychomotor delay, hypotonia, microcephaly, intractable seizures and autistic behavior, such as repetitive behaviors and lack of eye contact.; 3. Adenylosuccinate lyase deficiency type II, a more moderate form, typically does not result in signs or symptoms until after the first few years of life, resulting in mild to moderate psychomotor delay, seizures and autistic behavior. ; Small elevations of succinyladenosine in spinal fluid have also been reported in AICA-Ribosiduria (deficiency of AICAR transformylase) a devastating condition involving profound intellectual disability, epilepsy, dysmorphic features and congenital blindness. Small elevations are also seen secondary to fumarase deficiency.

fields.limitations: Note: Bloody CSF and samples received thawed may compromise analyte stability and lead to inaccurate results. Results should be interpreted in the context of clinical findings and other laboratory data. If results are inconsistent with the clinical presentation, consultation with the laboratory is recommended.
